content.text: I couldn't open any files, so this diagnosis comes from the repository layout and the usual structure of this NestJS boilerplate. The line numbers are estimates, not read from the code.

candidates.explanation: The refresh flow does not invalidate the old refresh token. The session hash that is embedded in the refresh token is either not compared with the stored session hash (`session.hash !== data.hash` is missing or wrong), or a new hash is generated but never persisted with `sessionService.update(session.id, { hash })`. The new tokens may also be signed with the old hash. Either way, the old refresh token still matches the session and can be replayed to get new token pairs.

If the session update does not actually write the new `hash` (for example the field is dropped by the mapper or the payload), the stored hash stays unchanged after rotation. The old refresh token then remains valid. The document repository and its mapper could have the same problem.

The refresh strategy only checks that the payload carries a session ID. It does not check the session hash. This is a lower-probability cause, because the hash comparison normally happens in AuthService.refreshToken.

fix.description: In refreshToken, load the session and throw UnauthorizedException if it is missing or if session.hash !== data.hash. Then generate a new random hash and persist it with `await this.sessionService.update(session.id, { hash })` before issuing tokens. Sign the new tokens with that new hash so the old refresh token no longer matches. Also make sure the session repository update writes the hash field.

candidates.explanation: The refresh flow does not invalidate the old refresh token. The session hash that is embedded in the refresh token is either not compared with the stored session hash (`session.hash !== data.hash` is missing or wrong), or a new hash is generated but never persisted with `sessionService.update(session.id, { hash })`. The new tokens may also be signed with the old hash. Either way, the old refresh token still matches the session and can be replayed to get new token pairs.

If the session update does not actually write the new `hash` (for example the field is dropped by the mapper or the payload), the stored hash stays unchanged after rotation. The old refresh token then remains valid. The document repository and its mapper could have the same problem.

The refresh strategy only checks that the payload carries a session ID. It does not check the session hash. This is a lower-probability cause, because the hash comparison normally happens in AuthService.refreshToken.

fix.description: In refreshToken, load the session and throw UnauthorizedException if it is missing or if session.hash !== data.hash. Then generate a new random hash and persist it with `await this.sessionService.update(session.id, { hash })` before issuing tokens. Sign the new tokens with that new hash so the old refresh token no longer matches. Also make sure the session repository update writes the hash field.
